title: Bundles, Product Rules & Configuration

toc.text: The Group: Option convention and option groups
Product rules: the four constraint types

html:
Phase 02 gave you a flat catalog; this phase makes it configurable. The heart of any CPQ implementation is the bundle: one sellable parent assembled from option lines, guarded by rules that make invalid combinations impossible and required combinations unavoidable. Everything in this module runs through BundleConfigurationService — the Apex class that validates bundle shape, detects conflicting options, and rolls up bundle prices.

The concepts here map 1:1 onto the real CPQ configurator (option groups, features, product rules of type Selection / Validation / Price) but using only the standard and custom data model from the spec, so you can practice in a plain Developer org.

Learning objectives

  • Define a bundle and its two line roles: parent (Is_Bundle_Parent__c = true) and option (Bundle_Option__c populated).
  • Explain the Group: Option naming convention and why it lets you simulate option groups.
  • Enumerate the four product-rule types (Selection, Validation, Price, Filter) and what each prevents.
  • Use BundleConfigurationService.validateBundleConfiguration to catch orphan options and empty parents.
  • Detect mutually-exclusive options with hasConflictingOptions.
  • Compute a bundle price with rollupBundlePrice without double counting the parent.
  • Contrast bundle modeling here with the SBQQ__ProductFeature__c / SBQQ__Option__c hierarchy.
  • Apply configuration boundaries: required, single-select, exclusion, and price-adjustment constraints.
  • Extend a validated bundle into the pricing and approval phases of the roadmap.

Bundles and option lines

A bundle is not a product — it is a relationship between quote lines. In this data model you flag the parent line and give option lines a value:

apex
QuoteLineItem parent = new QuoteLineItem(
    QuoteId = q.Id,
    PricebookEntryId = bundleEntry.Id,
    Is_Bundle_Parent__c = true,
    Quantity = 10, UnitPrice = 0,
    List_Unit_Price__c = 0, Net_Unit_Price__c = 0
);

QuoteLineItem option = new QuoteLineItem(
    QuoteId = q.Id,
    PricebookEntryId = cpuEntry.Id,
    Bundle_Option__c = 'CPU: Intel i7',
    Quantity = 10, UnitPrice = 600,
    List_Unit_Price__c = 600, Net_Unit_Price__c = 600
);

The two rules enforced by validateBundleConfiguration are the minimal contract of any bundle:

  1. A parent with no option line is an empty shell (invalid).
  2. An option line with no parent is an orphan (invalid).
apex
List<String> violations = BundleConfigurationService.validateBundleConfiguration(lines);
// empty list = valid bundle shape
Tip — In real CPQ the same two checks are distribution rules and option-count constraints. Whenever a quote "loses" products, suspect rule invalidation first: lines that violate a constraint are removed or deactivated, not just flagged.

The Group: Option convention and option groups

Single-select is the most common configuration constraint ("choose exactly one CPU tier"). Real CPQ models this as one option group with multiple options, selectable once. This project simulates the group with a prefix on the option value:

text
CPU: Intel i5      -> group = "CPU", value = "Intel i5"
CPU: Intel i7      -> group = "CPU", value = "Intel i7"
Storage: 100 GB    -> group = "Storage", value = "100 GB"
Storage: 500 GB    -> group = "Storage", value = "500 GB"

hasConflictingOptions picks the group by splitting on the colon and returns true if two different values land inside the same group:

Lines on the quoteResult
CPU: i5 + CPU: i7❌ conflict, returns true
CPU: i5 + Storage: 100 GB✅ different groups, no conflict
Two identical Storage: 500 GB rows✅ same value, not a conflict
apex
Boolean conflict = BundleConfigurationService.hasConflictingOptions(lines);
if (conflict) {
    System.debug('Pick exactly one option per group.');
}

Product rules: the four constraint types

A full configurator enforces more than single-select. These are the canonical rule types — you will see all four in real product rules and on the CPQ Specialist blueprint:

Rule typePrevents / forcesExample
SelectionWhich options may be selected togetheri9 only compatible with 32 GB+ RAM
ValidationRejects a configuration at quote timeServer requires an OS option
PriceAdjusts the price based on selectionsChoosing 500 GB disk adds +200
FilterRestricts which products appear as optionsOnly active, in-stock CPUs listed

In this project: selection/validation are the validateBundleConfiguration + hasConflictingOptions checks; price is rollupBundlePrice. Filter logic is represented by the IsActive = true guard when option entries are resolved.

When your client says "we need a rule that says X can't go with Y," the consultant translation is: which rule type, at which point (selection time or quote validation), and with which message?

Configurable attributes

Beyond line-level options, products expose attributes — the configurable dimension of a single product. Attributes answer "which flavor of this product," where options answer "which products go in this bundle." Typical attributes: color, storage tier, locale, max users.

In this learning model you can capture attributes as choice options on the line itself. A clean rule:

  • One feature/attribute → one group prefix.
  • The number of attributes you can configure on a product should be bounded — infinite attributes make validation and document generation impossible to scale.

Bundle price roll-up

A bundle's price is the sum of its selected options, not the parent's list price. rollupBundlePrice implements exactly that with a deliberate subtlety:

apex
public static Decimal rollupBundlePrice(List<QuoteLineItem> lines) {
    Decimal total = 0;
    Boolean hasOptions = false;
    for (QuoteLineItem li : lines) {
        if (String.isNotBlank(li.Bundle_Option__c)) { hasOptions = true; break; }
    }
    for (QuoteLineItem li : lines) {
        Decimal qty = li.Quantity == null ? 1 : li.Quantity;
        Decimal net = li.Net_Unit_Price__c != null
                      ? li.Net_Unit_Price__c
                      : (li.UnitPrice != null ? li.UnitPrice : 0);
        if (li.Is_Bundle_Parent__c == true && hasOptions) {
            continue;                    // parent price is replaced by the option roll-up
        }
        total += qty * net;
    }
    return total.setScale(2, System.RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
}

Why the hasOptions guard? If the parent is the only line (empty shell — which validation rejected above), the function still returns the parent's own net price as a fallback rather than silently returning zero. That is defensive coding: never let a roll-up wipe a price because of a missing companion line.

Worked example (quantity 10):

LineList unitNet unitParent?Option?Contributes
Bundle shell00✅–0 (skipped)
CPU: i5 (800)800760–✅7,600
Storage: 100 GB (200)200180–✅1,800
Bundle total9,400

Configuration boundaries worth enshrining

Production configurators fail on these rules first. Bake them into the design:

  • Required vs optional options — decide per feature. Optional features need "None" as an allowed selection, or the rule engine can't represent "the buyer declined."
  • Bounded option counts — min/max per group (e.g. 1–2 warranty options). Route conflicts to a validation message, never a hard SOQL failure.
  • Price constraints are not inventory checks — a price rule that says "add 200" is different from a selection rule that says "can't." Keep the four rule types separate or later modules won't be able to explain the behavior.
  • Defaults using group conventions — if the configurator preselects an option, represent it as an ordinary option line, not a special field.

Contrast: bundles in classic CPQ (SBQQ)

The legacy package models the same ideas with dedicated objects:

Concept hereClassic CPQ equivalent
Bundle parentSBQQ__QuoteLine__c with SBQQ__Bundle__c = true
Product featureSBQQ__ProductFeature__c (a configurable attribute of a product)
Option under a featureSBQQ__Option__c with price adjustment fields
Selection / validation ruleSBQQ__ProductRule__c, type Selection / Validation
Price ruleSBQQ__ProductRule__c, type Price
Option filteringSBQQ__OptionFilter__c

Translation skill: when you interview on a classic CPQ org, "option groups" mean features/options; when you implement on RLM, the same logic moves into the ProductSellingModel. The Apex logic in BundleConfigurationService is engine-agnostic — that is the point of the Academy.

When configuration rules run

A subtle product-rules fact: configuration validation is a snapshot at the line level, not a one-time event. Rules re-evaluate when lines change:

  1. Line inserted → shape + group checks run against the quote's full line set.
  2. Line changed (Bundle_Option__c, quantity) → group conflicts re-checked.
  3. Line deleted → a bundle can drop below its minimum; the empty-parent rule catches it.
  4. Quote recalculated → QuoteCalculatorService re-prices from the surviving lines.

That is why the walkthrough below always passes the whole line list to validateBundleConfiguration — a partial line set gives a false sense of validity.

Hands-on walkthrough

Build a configurable workstation bundle and put every service method through its paces.

  1. Create the catalog pieces (Phase 02 pattern) — a bundle shell plus two single-select option groups:

    apex
    List<Product2> products = [
    SELECT Id FROM Product2 WHERE ProductCode IN ('HW-WS-BUNDLE','HW-CPU','HW-DISK')
];
List<PricebookEntry> entries = [SELECT Id, Product2.ProductCode FROM PricebookEntry
                                WHERE Product2.ProductCode IN ('HW-WS-BUNDLE','HW-CPU','HW-DISK')];

    If you don't have them, insert the products and entries first (reuse Anon Apex from Phase 02) so the price book resolves.

  2. Open a quote on the standard price book and insert the shell + one option from each group:

    apex
    Quote q = new Quote(Name = 'Q-BUNDLE', OpportunityId = [SELECT Id FROM Opportunity LIMIT 1].Id,
    Pricebook2Id = [SELECT Id FROM Pricebook2 WHERE IsStandard = true LIMIT 1].Id);
insert q;

    Now insert lines: shell (Is_Bundle_Parent__c = true) and two options (CPU: Intel i7, Storage: 500 GB), each with list and net prices and quantity 10.

  3. Validate the shape — the parent + option count must satisfy both rules:

    apex
    List<QuoteLineItem> lines = [SELECT Id, Is_Bundle_Parent__c, Bundle_Option__c, Quantity,
                                    UnitPrice, List_Unit_Price__c, Net_Unit_Price__c
                             FROM QuoteLineItem WHERE QuoteId = :q.Id
                             ORDER BY Bundle_Option__c NULLS LAST];
System.debug(BundleConfigurationService.validateBundleConfiguration(lines)); // []

  4. Break it on purpose. Insert a second CPU option (CPU: Intel i5), then assert the conflict is detected — this is your single-select constraint:

    apex
    insert new QuoteLineItem(QuoteId = q.Id, PricebookEntryId = cpuEntry.Id,
    Bundle_Option__c = 'CPU: Intel i5', Quantity = 10, UnitPrice = 800,
    List_Unit_Price__c = 800, Net_Unit_Price__c = 760);
System.assertEquals(true, BundleConfigurationService.hasConflictingOptions(
    [SELECT Bundle_Option__c, Is_Bundle_Parent__c FROM QuoteLineItem WHERE QuoteId = :q.Id]));

  5. Roll up the price after deleting the rogue line:

    apex
    delete [SELECT Id FROM QuoteLineItem WHERE QuoteId = :q.Id AND Bundle_Option__c = 'CPU: Intel i5'];
List<QuoteLineItem> clean = [SELECT Is_Bundle_Parent__c, Bundle_Option__c, Quantity,
                                    UnitPrice, List_Unit_Price__c, Net_Unit_Price__c
                             FROM QuoteLineItem WHERE QuoteId = :q.Id];
Decimal bundlePrice = BundleConfigurationService.rollupBundlePrice(clean);
System.debug('Bundle price (option roll-up): ' + bundlePrice);
// 10 x 600 (CPU) + 10 x 200 (Storage) with nets 560/180 -> 5600 + 1800 = 7,400

  6. Feed the price upstream. Normalize the bundle into quote totals with the calculator service:

    apex
    QuoteCalculatorService.recalculateTotals(new Set<Id>{ q.Id });
Quote check = [SELECT Id, Total_ARR__c, Discount_Percent__c FROM Quote WHERE Id = :q.Id];
System.debug('Quote total after bundle roll-up: ' + check.Total_ARR__c);

  7. Guard-test the boundaries — the services must stay quiet on null/empty input:

    apex
    System.assertEquals(0, BundleConfigurationService.validateBundleConfiguration(null).size());
System.assertEquals(false, BundleConfigurationService.hasConflictingOptions(null));
System.assertEquals(0, BundleConfigurationService.rollupBundlePrice(new List<QuoteLineItem>()));

Common pitfalls

  • Validating a partial line set. Rules only see what you pass in; a single-option check passes while a second conflicting option hides in the DB. Always read the whole quote's lines.
  • Double counting the parent. Pricing the shell at 1000 and summing its options at 2000 yields 3000. rollupBundlePrice skips the parent when options exist for exactly this reason.
  • Group name hopes. The splitter keys on Group: Option. CPU: i5 groups as CPU; Intel i5 (no colon) groups as the whole string and never conflicts. Enforce the convention everywhere.
  • Same-value duplicates treated as conflicts. Two identical Storage: 500 GB rows are the same value in one group — allowed. Only distinct values within a group conflict.
  • Option lines without a quote. Every option line must carry the same QuoteId as its parent or it is invisible to the whole-quote validation and the roll-up.
  • Ignoring IsActive when building options. A deactivated product still resolves via a stale PricebookEntry. Option lists must be filtered IsActive = true to mirror filter rules.

Key takeaways

  • A bundle is two line roles: parent (Is_Bundle_Parent__c) and option (Bundle_Option__c), validated by validateBundleConfiguration.
  • The Group: Option convention simulates option groups, and hasConflictingOptions enforces single-select.
  • Four rule types (Selection, Validation, Price, Filter) cover all configuration constraints; this project implements the first three in Apex and the last as an active-check.
  • rollupBundlePrice sums selected options and never double-counts the parent — with a fallback so an empty shell never prices at zero.
  • Configuration rules re-run on every line change, so always validate the full line set.
  • The same logic exists as SBQQ__ProductFeature__c / SBQQ__Option__c / SBQQ__ProductRule__c in classic CPQ and inside ProductSellingModel in RLM.
  • A valid, rolled-up bundle is exactly the input the pricing phase needs — next up: price books, price rules, discount schedules, and block pricing.
